PGE (PGE-PL): a better business, heading into lower earnings per share

Investment memo for Richard. Written 15 November 2026.

Money is in zloty (PLN). Forecasts are the Financial Analyst's model (update 2); "the brokers" means the FactSet median. Definitions, prices and dates of the figures are in the end notes. PGE reports its third quarter on 24 November, after this memo was written.

#0Summary of key insights, implications and conclusions

PGE is becoming a better business and a weaker earnings-per-share story at the same time, and the share price so far reflects only the better business.

The group outside coal grows its EBITDA about 6% a year, and management runs it sensibly. PGE's earnings per share nonetheless fall every year to FY2029, and the shares are priced on brokers' estimates that do not yet show that fall.

The seven things to know

EBITDA stays flat while EPS halves. EBITDA holds between PLN 13.4bn and 14.0bn to FY2028, then drops to about PLN 12.3bn in FY2029. FY2029 is the first year after the coal fleet's capacity payments end in December 2028 (the "coal cliff"). EPS falls from PLN 2.80 in FY2026 to PLN 1.41 in FY2029.
Two-thirds of the EPS fall is already scheduled. Depreciation, interest and tax on a debt-funded building programme account for PLN 0.95 of the PLN 1.39 decline. Only the remaining third depends on coal, the uncertain part.
New EBITDA costs PGE's shareholders a lot; lost coal EBITDA costs them in full. The Baltica 2 offshore wind farm adds about PLN 1.1bn of EBITDA but roughly nothing to EPS in its first full year, because the wind farm brings its own depreciation and interest. Coal's lost EBITDA reaches EPS in full, because the coal fleet was written down in 2025 and has almost no depreciation left to shed.
The valuation calendar does the damage. At about 6.5 times the brokers' two-year-forward EPS of PLN 2.40, PGE's shares look cheap. By the end of 2027, however, the earnings two years forward will be FY2029's. On our FY2029 EPS of PLN 1.41, today's price is about 11 times earnings, the top of PGE's five-year range.
Expectations already contain the good news. We match the brokers on EBITDA to FY2028, and we sit below them on EPS by 3%, 8% and 10% for FY2026 to FY2028 and by 41% for FY2029. We are above the brokers only on the dividend (PLN 0.70 against PLN 0.55) and, slightly, on FY2026 EBITDA. I can find no path on which our assessment ends materially above what the market expects.
One variable can turn the return positive: state support for coal after 2028. For the shares to return nothing to the end of 2027 at the guideline multiple, coal support must reach about PLN 1.7bn a year, which would replace most of the capacity payments that expire. No such support has been proposed.
PGE's positives are real and worth keeping in view. About 60% of EBITDA is regulated or contracted, and that share rises every year. The first dividend since FY2015 is likely, and it is safer than credit commentary suggests. The balance sheet has room. Baltica 2 is on schedule. About half of the uncertainty in FY2027 earnings resolves on known dates before the end of December 2026.
-20.9%
The model's total return. At the guideline fair multiple of 8.64 times, the model gives a total return of minus 20.9% to 31 December 2027 and minus 19.4% to 30 June 2029 (#12).

Five judgements move PGE's value most (the arithmetic is in #6): the size of coal support after 2028; who pays for the government's 2027 cap on household power prices (the "shield"); the grid's allowed return; the schedule of depreciation, interest and tax; and how fast 2026's merchant margins fade.

Three developments would turn PGE into an investment case, in order of power. The first has no date, the second is a matter of price, and the third is not on the table.

#1Tailwinds and headwinds in the operating environment

Conclusion: the external environment is a strong tailwind for 2026 and early 2027, and it turns into a net headwind as coal capacity payments expire and the state looks for revenue.
Evidence

Three supports coincide in 2026

  • A gas-price shock. European gas prices rose 34% in the first half of 2026 and made coal and gas plants profitable again. PGE's second-quarter EBITDA rose 21% and its generation 18%.
  • Contracted capacity payments. Five-year contracts pay the coal fleet until December 2028, and a one-year supplementary award (1,859 MW, about PLN 0.6bn) covers 2027.
  • Grid demand. PGE signed 28,400 grid connection agreements in the first half, and its regulated asset base (the invested capital on which the regulator allows a return) grows about 9% a year.

Four headwinds stand against them

  • Affordability politics. Poland's budget deficit is near 7% of GDP, and a parliamentary election falls in autumn 2027. The state has already done three things: it demanded an extra PLN 265m from PGE under the 2022 to 2024 scheme that made generators pay for household price caps; it drafted a 2027 gas price cap paid for by a levy on the gas trader; and it passed a rise in corporate tax from 19% to 22% through the Senate. A further draft bill (UD459) would lift tax for large fuel and energy companies to 30% in 2027; on the published draft, integrated distribution and lignite mining fall outside that bill.
  • A falling grid return. The base allowed return on the grid is fixed at 7.478% for 2023 to 2028. The regulator sets a "reinvestment premium" on top of the base return each year and is cutting that premium: PGE's total allowed return is about 2.5 points lower in 2026 than the 12.96% of 2025.
  • Bond yields. Because the grid's base return is fixed, the rise in Polish ten-year yields to about 6.4% raises PGE's cost of new debt (6.5% to 7%) without raising what the grid may earn before 2029.
  • Solar and batteries. Poland has 25.6 GW of solar capacity and had more than 450 hours of negative power prices in 2025. The gas shock paused the displacement of coal by solar; it did not end it.
Inference

Each 2026 tailwind is temporary: the gas shock is cyclical, the capacity payments expire, and the grid's growth is capped by the regulator. The headwinds, by contrast, are structural or already dated. The 2026 windfall reaches PGE's 2027 earnings through forward power prices, in the same year that the state presents its political bill.

So what. The environment supports EBITDA for the next 12 months and is at its most favourable now. The same environment does not support EPS growth, and it gets harder from 2028.
Strongest counter-case. Energy security is moving coal's way. The State Assets minister said on 5 November that coal plants "could stabilise Poland's power system for years to come", and the grid operator is in talks with Brussels. The European Commission approved strategic reserves for Estonia (EUR 750m) and Sweden (EUR 300m) in 2025, so a legal template for supporting reserve plants exists. And in 2023 to 2025, household price caps came with prompt compensation to suppliers.

What would change my view. A household shield funded from the budget with no call on generators, a reinvestment premium held at its 2026 level in the December tariff, and a coal support framework with a number attached.

Against the market. The market read 2026 as a windfall for owners of existing plants and grids, and I agree. I differ on how long the windfall persists: the brokers carry coal EBITDA of PLN 2.1bn into FY2027 (the broker BOS has PLN 2.6bn), where the model has PLN 1.45bn.

Score: 35, set by the Rater. The 2026 supports are cyclical (a 34% gas shock), expiring (coal capacity payments end December 2028, a PLN 2-2.5bn a year revenue loss that reaches EPS in full) or regulator-capped (9% asset-base growth against a reinvestment premium cut about 2.5 points and a base return fixed while yields rise), while enacted fiscal take (corporate tax to 22%, the extra PLN 265m) and solar displacement are structural; consensus sales and EPS growth at the 3rd-4th percentiles confirm the turn, so over two to three years the environment is a clear net headwind on the business as it will be, a little below the External change forces group's 40 because the coal cliff falls inside the window. It sits below Fevertree (38), whose environment is merely flat, and just above Zegona (33), since the grid's connection-driven demand is a real structural positive on about 41% of EBITDA.

#2Internally driven corporate change

Conclusion: PGE's corporate change is positive in direction and well funded, but it reaches only the regulated half of the group and leaves untouched the coal half, which sets the earnings path.
Evidence

Management is improving what it controls

  • A coherent strategic reset. The October 2026 strategy, the first under Dariusz Lubera (President since January 2026), cut capital spending to 2035 from PLN 235bn to PLN 210bn and cut the 2030 EBITDA target from PLN 17bn to PLN 15bn. It made new gas plants conditional on capacity support after 2028 and put networks first. More than 70% of spending is to be backed by regulated returns or by contracts for difference (long-term, inflation-indexed fixed prices).
  • A dividend. Payments resume from FY2026 earnings, with a yield of "up to 5%".
  • Delivery. Baltica 2 (1.5 GW, half owned with Ørsted) had all 111 foundations installed by August and was 45% complete at the third quarter, with its PLN 30bn budget unchanged.
  • Funding. PLN 12.8bn of state-linked loans at 0.5% interest remain undrawn.

Coal and ownership remain untouched

  • Coal and governance have not changed. The plan to move coal plants to a state agency was cancelled in July 2025. PGE has had three presidents in 23 months. Executive pay is capped near PLN 0.75m with no equity component. Strategies are rewritten every 12 to 18 months, each time after a change of minister.
  • The coal efficiency programme is unproven. Management's 2030 coal loss of PLN 3.3bn already assumes an efficiency programme at the coal subsidiary that removes about PLN 1.8bn of losses. The programme has no published measures, staffing plan or closure schedule.
Inference

Management is improving what it controls: the quality of new capital and the delivery of contracted projects. Management cannot settle what sets the valuation, which is coal and ownership. Internal change is therefore raising PGE's earnings quality, not its earnings per share.

So what. I trust the contracted items in the forecasts (Baltica 2, the Rybnik gas plant and the batteries). I expect no positive surprise on costs or coal from management's own efforts.
Strongest counter-case. The dividend marks a real change in how the state treats PGE: for now, the state wants cash from the company, which is what minority shareholders want too. And management published its PLN 3.3bn coal loss while negotiating for support, so it had reason to show a large hole; the true unsupported coal loss may be smaller.

What would change my view. A published closure and staffing plan for the coal subsidiary with state-funded social costs (RWE received EUR 2.6bn and LEAG EUR 1.75bn for the same task in Germany), a stated dividend payout ratio, or a reduction of the state's stake.

Against the market. Bernstein's reading, "evolution, not revolution, and the dividend is back", is the prevailing one, and I share it. The market treats the October reset as the start of an earnings story; I see a better business mix on a falling EPS line.

Score: 46, set by the Rater. The October 2026 reset is coherent and funded (capex to 2035 cut PLN 25bn, over 70% of spending regulated or backed by contracts for difference, the first dividend since FY2015, Baltica 2 on budget, PLN 12.8bn of 0.5% loans), but it raises earnings quality rather than earnings: the debt-funded build brings depreciation and interest that take about PLN 0.87 off EPS by FY2029, the PLN 1.8bn coal efficiency programme has no published measures, and three presidents in 23 months with strategies rewritten every 12-18 months show churn; the 81st-percentile three-year margin change is the 2024-26 energy windfall, not self-help. I agree with the group's 47 that this is gently positive in direction but slightly net negative in its effect on EPS within three years, placing it just above Indus Holding (45) and below Reply (51).

#3Industry structure, business model, financial profile and management

Conclusion: PGE combines a state-granted grid monopoly and a strong balance sheet with average returns, negative cash flow, no pricing power and an owner whose interests match minority shareholders' only for now.
Evidence
  • Market position. PGE is first in Polish generation (about a third of national output) and in retail supply, and second in distribution (5.9 million customers across about 40% of the country).
  • EBITDA mix. FY2026 EBITDA is about 41% distribution, 18% district heating, 14% coal, 13% renewables, 9% railway energy, 8% gas and 1% supply.
    Distribution 41%
    Heating 18%
    Coal 14%
    Renewables 13%
    Rail 9%
    Gas 8%
  • Pricing. Every price PGE charges is set by the regulator, an auction or the power exchange. Households are supplied below cost, and business customers are leaving for their own generation.
  • Returns and cash. Post-tax return on capital is about 11% to 12% in FY2026, flattered by a coal fleet written down by almost PLN 9bn in 2025, and heads to about 8% by 2030. New capital earns 6% to 9% against a cost of equity of 11% to 12%. Free cash flow is negative in every forecast year.
  • Earnings quality. PGE's "non-recurring" charges recur at PLN 0.3bn to 0.8bn a year, so reported EPS runs PLN 0.10 to 0.27 below adjusted EPS.
  • Governance. The state holds 60.86% of the shares, and every other shareholder is capped at 10% of the votes. The state cut a proposed dividend from PLN 0.92 to PLN 0.25 in 2016 and backed a 20% share issue in 2022. PGE has never bought back a share.
  • Management. PGE's management out-executes its Polish peers on auctions and gas plants and runs the lowest leverage of the group. It trails the peers on smart meters and collections. Its stretch goal of EBITDA above PLN 30bn by 2035, about twice Bernstein's PLN 16bn, reflects the state's ambition more than a commercial plan, and the company culture is union-dense and built for stability.
Inference

PGE owns one excellent asset, a grid monopoly that grows with every new connection, alongside a strong balance sheet and a capable project organisation. These strengths sit inside an ownership structure that sets every price and has repeatedly put policy before minority shareholders. Barriers to entry are absolute in the grid and absent in generation, where private solar has taken 10 to 15 points of market share in five years.

So what. PGE is a medium-quality business with a high-quality core. At Bernstein's 7 times EBITDA, the grid alone is worth about PLN 38bn, a little more than the whole group's market value of about PLN 35bn, before net debt, provisions and the coal liability. The grid's value stays locked inside the group while coal and ownership are unchanged.

Strongest counter-case. Greece's Public Power Corporation re-rated from a distressed state utility to 14.6 times earnings. That re-rating needed the state's stake below 34%, a lignite exit by 2026 and one chief executive for seven years. PGE has the grid and the balance sheet but none of those three conditions.

What would change my view. Separation of coal from the group, a lower state stake, or equity-linked pay for management.

Against the market. The market gives PGE the lowest P/E in its sector, and on business foundations I think that low multiple is right. My difference with the market lies in the earnings to which the low multiple is applied (#6).

Score: 36, set by the Rater. Qualitatively PGE owns one fortress (a state-granted grid monopoly growing with 28,400 connections a half) beside generation with no barriers (private solar took 10-15 points of share), retail supplied below cost, every price administered, and an owner-regulator with a record of putting policy before minorities (the 2016 dividend cut, the 2022 issue, three presidents in 23 months, capped pay, a union-dense culture). Financially, reported return on invested capital of -6.4% (4th percentile) is a write-down artefact, but the better test is worse than it looks: new capital earns 6-9% against an 11-12% cost of equity and free cash flow is negative every forecast year. That is a good unit tied to weak ones, coherent with the groups (50, 45, 28, 25), between Teqnion (39) and Zegona (34).

#4Guidance, expectation management and the record of delivery

Conclusion: PGE is an honest tracker of its business, with no near-term guidance to beat, targets above our figures, and one conservative expectation, the dividend.
Evidence
  • PGE gives no annual guidance. PGE publishes 2030 and 2035 targets, and it releases preliminary quarterly figures about ten days before each report. It gives no bridge from EBITDA to EPS.

  • The delivery record. Against the brokers' EBITDA, PGE beat by roughly 2% to 6% in FY2022 to FY2024 and missed by about 9% in FY2025 (approximate comparisons, since there is no guidance). The first two quarters of 2026 were in line. Against its own plans, PGE has fallen short repeatedly; the 2030 EBITDA target was cut within 16 months of being set.
  • Estimates. The brokers raised FY2027 EPS by 64% in three months. External conditions and the strategy update drove that upgrade, not company guidance.
Inference

PGE's guidance tracks reality and does not lead it. PGE's targets sit above the model everywhere except coal and the dividend, so its guidance is neither conservative nor managed. Because PGE guides nothing below EBITDA, each broker fills that gap alone: for FY2027, Trigon and Erste reach the same EPS of PLN 2.60 from EBITDA figures PLN 2bn apart.

So what. No part of PGE's return can come from "beat and raise". The dividend is the single commitment on which expectations are conservative.
Strongest counter-case. The 2030 target is hedged by its own composition. If coal support of PLN 1.5bn to 2bn a year arrives, management can report PLN 15bn of EBITDA in total even while the rest of the group falls short. And on 24 November management is likely to give a segment-by-segment view of 2027, as it did a year ago, which would be guidance in all but name.

What would change my view. Annual guidance, a stated dividend payout ratio, or a year-by-year EBITDA path to 2030.

Against the market. Commentary calls the 2030 target "in line with consensus" and realistic. I think the 2030 target is more likely to be cut than met as published: about 55% likely to be cut by the end of 2029, 35% likely to be met with the help of coal support, and under 10% likely to be raised.

Score: 36, set by the Rater. There is no annual guidance (neutral in itself); against the brokers PGE beat EBITDA by 2-6% in FY2022-24, missed by about 9% in FY2025 and was in line in the first half of 2026, but against its own plans it has fallen short repeatedly, the 2030 EBITDA target was cut from PLN 17bn to 15bn within 16 months, and the standing target still sits above the model's PLN 12.8bn, so it is more likely cut again (about 55%) than met. Only the dividend is guided conservatively, and the 64% three-month EPS upgrade came from conditions, not guidance; coherent with the Guidance (40) and Sell-side estimates (20) groups, this sits just below Fevertree (39) and above Solid State (30).

#5Pricing power, leverage, cost scope and feedback loops

Conclusion: PGE has no pricing power and negative earnings gearing for the next four years, so stable EBITDA turns into falling EPS.
Evidence
  • Pricing power: none of the commercial kind. PGE's prices are administered. The 2026 household tariff of PLN 495.16/MWh is below cost, and large business customers bought 15% to 25% less power in the first quarter.
  • Operating leverage: present in coal, and working in reverse. Group revenue is mostly pass-through (in 2024 revenue fell 33% while EBITDA rose 8%). The real operating leverage sits in lignite, where mine and plant costs are fixed and capacity payments are fixed revenue. When the capacity payments stop, the fixed costs stay: coal EBITDA swings from plus PLN 1.85bn in FY2026 to minus PLN 1.40bn in FY2029.
  • Capital leverage below EBITDA. Depreciation rises 40% between FY2026 and FY2030, and net financial costs triple.

A worked example: Baltica 2's first full year (PGE's half) against PLN 1bn of coal EBITDA

  • Costs. PGE can cut few costs by choice. Wages rise 5% to 6% a year under signed agreements, two-thirds of staff are union members, and plant closures need political consent. Capital spending is the one flexible cost line.
  • Feedback loops.

    One loop works for the equity

    Asset-base growth lifts regulated EBITDA, which lifts debt capacity, which funds more grid investment.

    Three loops work against the equity

    Fiscal stress leads the state to take more from PGE (tax, levies, dividend). Solar and batteries cut coal plants' running hours and raise their unit cost. Any windfall invites clawback, so PGE's upside is capped while its downside is not protected.
Inference

PGE's earnings are geared the wrong way for the next four years: more capital and flat EBITDA produce less EPS. The same gearing means that each zloty of coal support reaches EPS almost in full: PLN 1bn of EBITDA is PLN 0.33 a share, or 24% of FY2029 EPS.

So what. EBITDA beats will not convert into EPS upgrades of the same size. The equity's sensitivity is concentrated in coal and in policy.
Strongest counter-case. PGE's earnings gearing turns positive once the building programme passes its peak. After about 2030, depreciation and interest stop outrunning EBITDA, the regulated asset base keeps compounding, and the 0.5% state-linked loans save PLN 0.7bn to 0.8bn a year once drawn.

What would change my view. Capital spending falling toward the brokers' PLN 10.7bn for FY2028 without slower asset-base growth.

Against the market. Market commentary on PGE is conducted in EBITDA and business mix, and on those measures I agree with it. I have not found anyone who adds up the effect on EPS.

Score: 20, set by the Rater. The structure works against the equity: no commercial pricing power (every price administered, the household tariff below cost), revenue mostly pass-through, real operating leverage only in lignite where fixed mine and plant costs stay when the fixed capacity revenue stops (coal EBITDA from +PLN 1.85bn to -1.40bn), wages contracted up 5-6% a year with little cost-out by choice, and rising depreciation (+40%) and tripling interest turning flat EBITDA into halving EPS. The one reinforcing loop (asset base lifts debt capacity) feeds the grid, not EPS, before 2030, and the gearing to coal support is gearing to a price PGE cannot set, so it sits between the 25 and 10 levels, coherent with Economic strength (28) and Financial forecasts (15).

The scope for growth is limited, and the growth that exists is debt-funded

  • Double-digit growth is absent at group level. EBITDA excluding coal grows about 6% a year. Offshore wind goes from nothing to PLN 1.1bn of EBITDA, and distribution grows about 3% a year as a 9% annual increase in the asset base meets a falling allowed return.
  • Growth and margins are lower than in the past. EBITDA more than doubled between FY2021 and FY2025. Over the next four years EBITDA is flat to down, and the EBIT margin falls from 13.5% to about 9%.
  • Cash. Free cash flow totals about minus PLN 23bn over five years, so the dividend is paid from borrowing. The bank covenant of 3.5 times EBITDA excludes project finance and CO2 obligations; on the covenant's definition, leverage is about 1.6 to 2.5 times by 2029 to 2030, so the covenant does not bind. The dividend declines because EPS declines, at a payout of about 25% to 32% of the prior year's earnings.

The five judgements that move the value most, with the arithmetic

Rule of thumb: each PLN 1.0bn of EBITDA is PLN 745m after 25.5% tax, or PLN 0.33 a share on 2,243.7m shares.

1. Coal support after 2028. Base case: coal EBITDA of minus PLN 1.4bn in FY2029, after an assumed PLN 0.5bn a year of replacement support. The capacity revenue that stops is about PLN 2.0bn to 2.5bn a year.

  • Support of PLN 1.5bn (PLN 1.0bn above base): 1.0 x 0.33 = plus PLN 0.33. FY2029 EPS rises to 1.74 (+24%), EBITDA to PLN 13.25bn, and net debt is about PLN 0.75bn lower each year.
  • No support (PLN 0.5bn below base): 0.5 x 0.33 = minus PLN 0.17. FY2029 EPS falls to 1.24 (-12%).
  • Management's coal loss profile (about PLN 1.0bn worse than base in FY2029, my scaling of management's 2030 figure): FY2029 EPS falls to 1.08 (-24%), EBITDA to PLN 11.25bn, and net debt to EBITDA is 2.7 times instead of 2.4 on the model's definition.
  • Coal at break-even (PLN 1.4bn above base): plus PLN 0.46. FY2029 EPS of 1.87 is still 22% below the one broker's 2.39. Reaching the broker's 2.39 needs support of about PLN 3.5bn a year, more than the capacity payments being lost.

2. Who pays for the 2027 household price shield. Base case: a price cap with compensation from the budget and no levy on generators. A levy or revenue cap on generators has a 25% to 35% chance.

  • A PLN 1.0bn levy: minus PLN 0.33. FY2027 EPS falls to 2.07 (-14%) and EBITDA to PLN 12.4bn; free cash flow is about PLN 0.75bn worse; and the dividend paid in 2028, at the model's 27% payout, is about PLN 0.56 instead of 0.65.
  • Adding a household tariff set PLN 0.3bn further below cost: a further minus PLN 0.10, to EPS of 1.97.
  • Adding a grid premium one point lower (PLN 0.25bn): a further minus PLN 0.08, to EPS of about 1.89 on EBITDA of PLN 11.8bn. This joint case has about one chance in ten, more than its parts' probabilities multiplied, because one cause (fiscal stress) drives all three.
  • If a levy lasts into 2029, as regional levies have lasted two to three years elsewhere: FY2029 EPS of 1.08.

3. The grid's allowed return. Base case: the total allowed return falls a little under one point a year, to about 8.5% by 2029. One point of allowed return is worth about PLN 0.25bn of EBITDA, or PLN 0.08 a share.

  • One to two points either way by FY2028: plus or minus PLN 0.25bn to 0.5bn of EBITDA, or PLN 0.08 to 0.17 a share (4% to 8% of FY2028 EPS).
  • The brokers' flat distribution EBITDA (PLN 5.27bn in FY2028, against the model's 5.75bn): minus PLN 0.48bn, or minus PLN 0.16 a share.

4. The schedule below EBITDA. Base case: depreciation of PLN 6.2bn and net financial costs of PLN 1.8bn in FY2029, with tax at 25.5% from FY2027.

  • The President vetoes the tax rise (about one chance in three; decision due by about 1 December): 2.5 points on FY2027 pre-tax profit of PLN 7.2bn is PLN 180m, or plus PLN 0.08 of EPS (+3%).
  • Capital spending at the brokers' pace in FY2027 and FY2028 (PLN 6.3bn less in total): interest at 5% saves PLN 0.3bn and depreciation about PLN 0.2bn, so pre-tax profit is PLN 0.5bn higher and FY2029 EPS is PLN 0.17 higher (+12%). Net debt is PLN 6.3bn lower, but asset-base growth is slower later.
  • Each five points of extra tax on the whole earnings base (the reach of draft bill UD459 is unsettled): minus PLN 0.16 of FY2027 EPS (-7%).

5. How fast 2026's merchant margins fade. Base case: coal and gas EBITDA fall PLN 0.65bn in FY2027.

  • The 2027 forward power price holds near PLN 590/MWh on unsold volume: plus PLN 0.4bn of EBITDA, or plus PLN 0.13 a share. FY2027 EPS rises to 2.53, close to the brokers' 2.60.
  • Gas and power prices fall back faster: minus PLN 0.5bn, or minus PLN 0.17, to EPS of 2.23.
  • The speed of the merchant-margin fade sets FY2027 EPS, the next dividend and the tone of 2027's quarterly results. It does not move FY2029, because the capacity payments end whatever power spreads do.
So what. The predictable part of the forecast (depreciation, interest and tax) is the part that lowers EPS. The uncertain part (coal and policy) decides by how much EPS falls.

I change no forecast input. The one input I would move next is FY2026 capital spending: the model's PLN 13.0bn needs second-half spending 25% to 30% above last year's. The third-quarter report will settle that question within days, and a change would shift cash between years without changing earnings.

Strongest counter-case. PGE's EPS decline is partly a matter of basis and timing. The brokers' own EBITDA, depreciation and financial lines, taxed at 25.5%, already produce about PLN 2.3 to 2.35 of FY2027 EPS, so part of the gap between the model and the brokers reflects stale medians, not a difference of view. And if capital spending runs lower, as it has so far in 2026, depreciation and interest arrive later.

What would change my view. Second-half distribution EBITDA near PLN 2.9bn (the model needs about 2.7bn), nine-month capital spending below about PLN 8bn, or a presidential veto of the tax rise.

Against the market. The brokers' forecasts show the same shape as the model's through FY2028, with less depth. The one visible broker FY2029 figure (EBITDA of PLN 14.1bn, EPS of 2.39) contains no coal cliff.

Score: 8, set by the Rater. Falling EPS gives F; consensus EPS growth of -4.2% (3.7th percentile) shows less depth than the model but the same sign. I place it near the floor because the decline is structural and largely scheduled (PLN 0.95 of the 1.39 fall is depreciation, interest and tax), the EBIT margin falls from 13.5% to about 9% against a doubling of EBITDA in FY2021-25, free cash flow is negative throughout, and there is no route back to the past EPS level within the horizon; only the 6% a year growth outside coal keeps it off the very bottom.

The likely path of revisions (my probabilities)

  • FY2026 EBITDA raised a little with the third quarter: about 60%. Tauron's preliminary third quarter beat consensus by 16% on 2 November, a mild positive read-across to PGE.

  • The dividend paid in 2027 raised: about 65%.

Two mechanical points work against the estimate momentum

  • The October upgrades leave FactSet's three-month revision window on about 21 January 2027 and the six-month window on about 21 April. The three-month revision figures therefore fade to about zero by February, whatever PGE reports.
  • After the FY2026 results (March to April 2027), brokers add FY2029 to their models. Spring 2027 is therefore when a broad market view of the first year without capacity payments first forms.

Scope for upgrades exists in two small places, FY2026 EBITDA and the dividend, and both upgrades are widely anticipated. The larger revisions ahead point down, and model refreshes and the calendar, not news, will trigger them. PGE's guidance cannot be raised because PGE gives none.

So what. The positive events of 2027 (the dividend proposal, vote and payment, and Baltica 2's first power) are not results events. PGE's results run mildly negative through 2027, with year-on-year growth returning only in the quarter reported in March 2028.
Strongest counter-case. There is about one chance in five that forward prices hold, no levy comes, the household tariff covers cost and the tax rise is vetoed. FY2027 EPS then reaches about PLN 2.7, which matches the brokers' estimate but does not exceed it.

What would change my view. Shield legislation that rules out a levy, and a tariff decision that lets PGE book a 2027 household provision well below the PLN 436m it booked for 2026. Erste expects a provision of about PLN 500m if tariffs are capped.

Against the market. The market narrative rests on the 2030 target, the dividend and a gradual re-rating of PGE as an infrastructure group. I agree with the first six months of that narrative, and I expect the EPS arithmetic to take over from spring 2027.

Score: 20, set by the Rater. Guidance, which counts most, cannot be raised (there is none annually) and the de facto 2030 target is more likely cut than met; consensus FY2027 EPS is 55-60% likely to be cut 5-10% (only 15-20% raised) against revenue growth of about nil, so the size ratio is strongly negative, and FY2028 sits 10% above the model as brokers add the FY2029 cliff from spring 2027 inside the window. The only upside is small and known (FY2026 EBITDA, the dividend at 0.70 against 0.55), and the narrative the memo expects to turn from spring 2027; coherent with the fourth-set group (22), between Prosus (22) and Yara (17).

#8Current momentum: guidance, estimates, narrative, price and peers

Conclusion: momentum in PGE's share price and estimates is strong now, but broker ratings have already turned, peers are weak, and the revision figures fade mechanically from late January 2027.
Evidence
  • Dashboard ratings (8 November). The Master Dashboard rates PGE A on technical momentum, A on sell-side earnings momentum, C on valuation and B on thematic fit.
    Technical momentum: ASell-side earnings momentum: AValuation: CThematic fit: B
  • Price. The shares are up 41% in three months and 40% in twelve, stand 38% above their 200-day average and 10% below their high of PLN 17.55, and rank at the 97th percentile on relative strength.
  • Estimates. Consensus FY2027 EPS is up 13% in one month, 64% in three and 49% in six. Consensus FY2027 EBITDA is up 13% in three months, so most of the EPS upgrade came from lines below EBITDA.
  • Ratings and targets. Buy ratings are 29% of the total, down 21 points in a month. The mean target price of PLN 15.56 is below the share price. Target prices run from PLN 9.30 to PLN 20.00.
  • Guidance. Guidance has no positive momentum: the last change to PGE's targets was a cut.
  • Peers. Tauron and Enea have technical momentum of D, earnings momentum of C and twelve-month returns of minus 9% and minus 1%. Energa's share price is pinned by Orlen's buyout. PGE's daily share price moves track Tauron's (correlation 0.80) and Enea's (0.70); the European utilities sector explains only 15% of them.
  • Investors: an evidence gap. The research found almost no direct evidence of who bought the rally or what holders say: there is no share register, fund-flow or short-interest data. I cannot judge the investor narrative from the files.
Inference

PGE's momentum is strong, specific to PGE and led by estimates, not by the multiple. A share price that followed three brokers' estimates up will follow those estimates down. The brokers have endorsed the higher numbers and stopped endorsing the higher price.

So what. Momentum supports the shares into the dividend proposal in March to April 2027. The momentum has an expiry date (the revision windows in #7), and peers give no support if it fades.
Strongest counter-case. Estimate-led rallies last while estimates rise, and the brokers Trigon and BOS already sit above the median on EBITDA. With Energa leaving the market, PGE is the liquid way to own Polish grids, which supports investor flows into the shares.

What would change my view. Fresh EPS upgrades after 24 November that come with new Buy ratings, or evidence that long-term domestic funds were the buyers.

Against the market. I agree with the market that PGE's momentum is strong today. I differ from the market on how long the momentum lasts.

Score: 82, set by the Rater. Both measures in the top fifth would give A, but two parts are negative: the last move on de facto guidance was a cut (2030 EBITDA from PLN 17bn to 15bn) and Buy ratings fell 21 points in a month to 29% (22nd percentile) with the mean target below the price, while peers Tauron and Enea are weak (D technical, C earnings momentum). So B, placed high in the band because the estimate and price momentum are exceptional (FY2027 EPS +64% in three months, 98.8th percentile; price 38% above its 200-day average).

#9Riskiness and simplicity of the case

Conclusion: the case is simple in structure, easy to track and fragile in outcome, because a few linked state decisions can move FY2029 EPS by anything from minus 20% to plus 45%.
Evidence
  • Simplicity. The structure of the case is simple: two earnings engines (the regulated grid and coal), each with dates. The numbers are not simple: there are four EPS bases, three definitions of net debt and eight segments. Every error found in the earlier research on PGE was an error of definition, so this memo states the definition beside each such figure.
  • Concentration. Three decision-makers set most of the outcome: the energy regulator, the State Treasury and the European Commission. Their choices are linked through affordability politics, so the downside drivers move together.
  • The range of outcomes widens with time.
-30%central+50% against central
FY2026 EBITDA
PLN 13.6bn; plus or minus 2.5%
FY2027 EBITDA
PLN 13.4bn; PLN 12.3bn to 14.1bn; probability-weighted about 13.1bn (violet)
FY2027 EPS
PLN 2.40; about PLN 1.9 to 2.7
FY2029 EPS
PLN 1.41; about PLN 1.1 to 2.1

The cone of outcomes: each bar spans the plausible range as a percentage of the central figure (black line). The further out the year, the wider the range, and the skew for FY2027 is downward.

  • Suddenness. A levy on generators can be announced on any day. The tariff and tax decisions are dated. Coal support has no clock.
  • Trackability. The case is easy to track for 18 months. PGE's onerous-contract provisions are its own estimate of next year's losses, booked in advance, and they are the best leading indicator PGE publishes.
  • Precedents at PGE. PGE's shares fell 21% in six months in 2013 (on a state-directed coal plant), 19% in late 2015 (on a coal-mine rescue), and with the sector in December 2024 when the coal carve-out came into doubt. In 2023 PGE paid PLN 6.6bn into the fund that financed household price caps.
  • Precedents for a dated loss of support. Tauron and Enea were de-rated ahead of the end of their capacity contracts in 2025, and Tauron's generation EBITDA then halved. In the cases researched, estimates showed the fall about 18 months ahead and multiples compressed 12 to 24 months ahead. For PGE's December 2028 expiry, that de-rating window opens now and runs through 2027.
Downside. PGE's median multiple (5.3 to 6.2 times) on FY2029 EPS gives a share price of PLN 7.5 to 8.7, a fall of 45% to 52%. Reference points: the 52-week low of PLN 8.21, Wood's target price of PLN 9.30 and Bernstein's sum-of-the-parts value of PLN 14.20.
Inference

PGE's risk is concentrated, correlated and negatively skewed for 18 months, and two-sided after that. Bad policy would hit earnings and the multiple together, because the Polish political factor in the share price has the same source as the earnings risk. The earnings risk and the multiple risk therefore do not diversify each other.

So what. PGE is a case to manage by the calendar. Seven weeks from now the tax rate, the grid premium, the household tariff and the shield design will be known, and the range of FY2027 outcomes will be about half as wide.
Strongest counter-case. The risks are known and dated, about 60% of EBITDA is regulated or contracted, leverage is the lowest among Polish peers, capital spending can flex by PLN 3bn to 5bn a year, and the state needs PGE to keep investing.

What would change my view. A household shield funded from the budget, and any coal framework that puts a clock and a number on post-2028 support.

Against the market. The brokers' ratings suggest they see the price risk. Their FY2029 numbers suggest they have not sized the earnings risk.

Score: 35, set by the Rater. The structure is simple and dated and trackable for 18 months, but the memo's FY2027 EPS cone of PLN 1.9-2.7 around 2.40 is about -21% to +12% and skewed down, FY2029 runs PLN 1.1-2.1, and the drivers are three linked state decision-makers (regulator, Treasury, Commission) whose choices move earnings and the multiple together; a generator levy can arrive on any day, the coal-support question has no clock, and precedents (Tauron and Enea de-rated 12-24 months before their capacity contracts ended, PGE's 19-21% falls on policy) point to a 45-52% downside at the median multiple. Low current leverage (0.4x) removes only solvency risk; this sits between OMV Petrom (44), whose fiscal-intervention risk is narrower, and Helios Towers (33), coherent with the Risks groups (30 and 45).

#10Where the stock is in its lifecycle

Conclusion: PGE is in late Broadening today, with Stalling the most likely next phase by mid-2027.
Evidence
  • The dashboard's rule places PGE in Broadening, because the share price, estimates and relative strength have risen together.
  • The signs of a later stage are present. The upgrades have been made and are dated. Ratings were cut as estimates rose. The next revisions lean down. Three quarters of year-on-year EBITDA decline are scheduled for 2027. FY2029, the year that carries the bad news, enters brokers' models in spring 2027.
  • PGE has no way to move into Reinforcing, because it gives no guidance to beat and raise.
  • PGE's earlier rallies ended on policy, not on results. Morgan Stanley called the 2014 rally "overdone" once the multiple stood at a premium to its history, and the 2021 and 2023 rallies faded when the coal carve-out stalled.
ReinforcingNo way in: no guidance to beat and raise

Inference

I read PGE as late Broadening, moving to Stalling during the first half of 2027 unless coal support arrives. A move to Collapsing would need a policy shock, such as a levy on generators or a refusal of coal support.

So what. The time to own a stock in late Broadening is short, and the events that sustain PGE's phase (the dividend proposal and Baltica 2's first power) are known and near.
Strongest counter-case. A Broadening thesis can widen further, from "energy windfall" to "regulated grid owner with a dividend", which is how Bernstein frames PGE. If investors value the better business mix and look through FY2029, the Broadening phase extends.

What would change my view. Estimates for FY2028 and FY2029 rising after brokers add the cliff year, or the multiple holding as quarterly EBITDA declines.

Against the market. The dashboard and the share price say Broadening. I expect the stock to be one stage later, in Stalling, six months from now.

Score: 32, set by the Rater. The computed Broadening reads price, estimates and relative strength rising together, but the rally rests on a gas-shock windfall: the upgrades are made, ratings were cut as estimates rose, the next revisions lean down, three quarters of year-on-year EBITDA decline are scheduled for 2027 and FY2029 enters models in spring. I agree with the memo's late Broadening moving to Stalling by mid-2027 and weigh it slightly more to Stalling, since nothing in the next six to twelve months broadens the earnings, placing it between D'Ieteren (35) and Imperial Brands (28).

#11The fair multiple

Conclusion: the guideline's 8.64 times is defensible as a generous multiple on trough-year earnings, and I would treat it as the top of a 6.2 to 8.6 times range until coal is resolved.

The guideline. Viewforth's guideline sets PGE's fair two-year-forward P/E at 8.64 times, the 80th percentile of PGE's ten-year history and the level for a stock in Broadening. The ten-year range is 3.8 times at the 10th percentile, 6.2 at the median, 8.1 at the 75th and 10.3 at the 90th.

My view: 8.64 times is a fair central figure, but for a different reason than the phase label gives.

  • On the phase alone, 8.64 times looks generous. I place the stock late in Broadening and heading for Stalling, which argues for a multiple between the median and the 75th percentile, 6.2 to 8.1 times.
  • On the earnings it is applied to, 8.64 times is reasonable. The model applies the multiple to FY2029 EPS, a cliff-year figure. Markets pay high multiples on depressed earnings: PGE's own multiple exceeded 13 times in late 2025 after the write-downs, and CEZ's rose to 23 times when its coal depreciation was accelerated.
  • The cross-check supports it. 8.64 times PLN 1.41 is PLN 12.2 a share. PLN 12.2 is 5.1 times FY2027 EPS and 5.5 times FY2028 EPS, close to PGE's five-year median of 5.3 times on nearer earnings. The guideline's value is therefore what PGE has usually been worth on earnings investors can see.
  • My range. 6.2 to 8.6 times FY2029 EPS, with 8.64 times at the top. A multiple above 10 times needs coal separated or supported; Public Power Corporation's 14.6 times shows what a completed coal exit earns.

Today's multiple has three readings, and one is unreconciled. The files give 6.4 to 6.6 times on the brokers' EPS (FactSet and the dashboard), 8.0 times on the model's own forward EPS at PLN 16.30, and 8.78 times on the Phases page (13 November). I could not reconcile the 8.78 times with the other two readings from the files. The total return does not depend on which reading is right, because the value at each horizon is the guideline multiple times that horizon's earnings. The split of the return does depend on it: on 8.78 times, the multiple contributes about minus 2% and earnings about minus 24%, where the model shows plus 8% and minus 31%.

The valuation window reaches the cliff year during 2027: about 6.5 times the brokers' EPS today is about 11 times FY2029 EPS.
Strongest counter-case. Bernstein values PGE's parts at PLN 14.20 a share, about 10 times FY2029 EPS, on the view that a group moving to 63% regulated and contracted EBITDA deserves a higher multiple over time.

What would change my view. Coal support of PLN 1.5bn a year or more would lift both the earnings and the multiple that fits them, toward the 90th percentile.

Against the market. At about 6.5 times the brokers' EPS, the market's multiple looks modest. On the model's earnings the same share price is already at the 75th percentile of PGE's range, and on FY2029 earnings it is above the 90th.

Score: 40, set by the Rater. Neutral on both would give C, but both readings rest on brokers' EPS that the memo puts 8-10% too high for FY2027-28 and 41% too high for FY2029; on the model's own forward EPS today's 8.0x is at about the 75th-80th percentile of the range and on FY2029 earnings above the 90th, and a stock heading from late Broadening into Stalling deserves less than its history, so the neutral reading flatters and I move the letter one step to D. Placed mid-band because the guideline 8.64x on trough earnings is defensible and the peer reading is genuinely neutral.

#12Total shareholder return

Conclusion: the model's return is about minus 20% on both horizons, driven by a 31% fall in forward earnings that the multiple and the dividend only partly offset, and only coal support of about PLN 1.7bn a year brings the return back to zero.

The model's return at the guideline multiple (share price PLN 16.30)

At the 6 November share price of PLN 15.755, the same values give total returns of minus 18.2% and minus 16.6%.

What drives the return

  • Earnings: minus 31%. The earnings two years forward fall from about PLN 2.04 today (PLN 16.30 divided by 8.0) to PLN 1.41 at the end of 2027, when the two-year-forward window covers FY2029. This fall in forward earnings is the EPS bridge in #6 seen through the valuation window.
  • The multiple: plus 8%. The multiple moves from 8.0 times to the guideline 8.64 times.
  • Dividends: plus 4%. PGE pays PLN 0.70 in mid-2027. The value of PLN 12.89 is a share price of about PLN 12.19 plus that dividend.
  • The longer horizon. The June 2029 horizon adds the PLN 0.65 dividend paid in 2028 and applies the multiple to earnings of about PLN 1.36. One more dividend offsets a little more earnings decline, so the total return barely changes.
  • The next six months. The model gives no return for a period this short. Nothing forces a de-rating before brokers add FY2029 in spring 2027, and today's share price is close to 6.5 times the brokers' PLN 2.40. The return over the next six months is therefore set by sentiment and the December decisions.

What would change the return (my arithmetic on the model's method: to 31 December 2027, from PLN 16.30, with the PLN 0.70 dividend)

Inference

The return is negative across the plausible range of outcomes and is driven by earnings; the guideline multiple already cushions it. Break-even needs FY2029 EPS of PLN 1.81, which means coal close to break-even in 2029 and support of about PLN 1.7bn a year. The one broker's case shows how much rests on FY2029: if that broker's FY2029 EPS of 2.39 is right, the same method gives a gain of about 31%.

Strongest counter-case. If the market keeps valuing PGE on a multiple of near-term earnings and looks through the coal cliff as a known, negotiable event, the 2027 dividend and a stable multiple give a small positive return over the next six to nine months.

What would change my view. Coal support of PLN 1.7bn a year or more, or evidence in spring 2027 that brokers model FY2029 EPS near PLN 2.

Against the market. The brokers' mean target price of PLN 15.56 implies a flat share price. The model's value is about 20% lower, and the whole difference is the earnings in the forward valuation window.

Score: 9, set by the Rater. A loss of about a fifth gives F, about 10 on the scale, and the three-year check confirms it, driven by a 31% fall in forward earnings that the multiple (+8%) and dividend (+4%) only partly offset. I move it down a point for the skew: the lower tail is fat and correlated (no coal support -30%, the median multiple -42%), while the only positive case needs one broker's FY2029 EPS or coal support of about PLN 1.7bn a year that has not been proposed.

#13Summary conclusion

PGE deserves respect as a business and caution as an equity at this price. The grid is a compounding monopoly, the balance sheet is the strongest among PGE's Polish peers, management delivers what is contracted, and the state currently wants what minority shareholders want: investment and a dividend. Those strengths make PGE a sound credit and an improving utility.

The equity case is weaker because of where PGE's earnings go and when the market will see it. EPS falls from PLN 2.80 to PLN 1.41 in three years, mostly for scheduled reasons. The shares rose 40% on estimates that stop a year short of the coal cliff, and the valuation window reaches the cliff year during 2027. The outcomes are skewed the wrong way for the setups Richard looks for: the upgrades have been made, the remaining positive surprises are small and known, and the one large positive, coal support, is also the best-known hope in the story.

The practical work is clear, and it follows the calendar.

December 2026Watch the tax, shield, tariff and capacity decisions, which halve the FY2027 uncertainty

No date

Short of a coal framework, FY2029 earnings are already paid for at a share price between PLN 8.7 and PLN 12.2 (6.2 to 8.64 times PLN 1.41).

20Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: 20, set by the Rater. The input forces are net negative (external 35, as the 2026 windfall fades and contracted capacity payments end; internal 46, a positive reset whose debt-funded build lowers EPS) and the output is decisive: EPS halves by FY2029 (F, 8), and two-thirds of the fall is already scheduled, so the negative change reaches profits with high certainty. Growth of about 6% a year outside coal keeps it off the 10 level, which needs strong negative change on both sides.
37Foundations' Robustness: 37, set by the Rater. A grid monopoly and today's low leverage, with about 60% of EBITDA regulated or contracted and rising, give real stability, but the business is a price-taker everywhere, earns 6-9% on new capital against an 11-12% cost of equity, burns cash every forecast year as net debt rises from PLN 7bn to 35bn, and is run by an owner-regulator with a record of policy before minorities (quality 36); the delivery record (36), with the 2030 target cut and likely cut again, adds nothing, so it sits between the 25 and 50 levels.
10Setups' Fit/Crispness: 10, set by the Rater. I agree with the memo's F: the case fits none of the setups in substance and is closer to the inverse of one, a windfall at its earnings high with a dated cause for concern (the coal cliff) ahead rather than clearing, alongside a business with no pricing power and falling EPS; the one development that would create a fit (a coal framework of about PLN 2bn a year) has no date and is not proposed.
30Case Riskiness: 30, set by the Rater. The case is simple to state and its dated decisions are trackable (riskiness 35), but the risk is concentrated in a few correlated state decisions that move earnings and the multiple together, the skew is negative for 18 months, and the share price is extended after an estimate-led 40% rally (38% above its 200-day average) with a 45-52% downside at the median multiple; that main risk of a large fall on a stretched, sentiment-carried price sits it below Richard's Arteche (60) and, with fundamental policy risk on top, below the typical case.

Appendix: a comment from the Financial Analyst on reporting basis

Our model keeps one reporting basis for history and forecasts. The checks below suggest that consensus may use a different basis for some lines, so part of the gap between our forecasts and consensus on those lines may not be a difference of view. Nothing has been adjusted in the model.

What the checks found:

  • FY2025 earnings per share: -3.10 on the brokers' basis against 3.00 on our model's basis (-203.2%).

Facts in the data file that commonly explain such a gap:

  • Non-controlling (minority) interests on the balance sheet: 1,240.0, 3.4% of market capitalisation. Our model does not deduct them; consensus earnings per share do.
  • Amortisation of acquired intangibles over the last twelve months: -317.0 before tax (-0.14 per share); our model's FY2025 history does not exclude it (its EBITA equals EBIT). Brokers' adjusted figures often exclude it.
  • Hybrid bond coupons and capitalised leases are not in the data file; check the company's reporting where relevant.

How to read this page

Every rating of this stock on one page: the Rater's 1-100 number, its letter and the Rater's own reason (at most three sentences, taken from the ratings file; nothing newly written). The number is the company's approximate standing in the Universe of about 1,300 listed European companies (90 = better than about 9 in 10; 50 = typical). A letter follows its item's rule: rank among the stocks scored (A the top 10%; B+ and B the next 15%; C+, C and C- the next 25%; D the next 25%; F the bottom 25%); or Richard's cut-offs on the measure for the four numerical topics (forecast financials, current momentum, the fair multiple, total shareholder return). On the change-forces items the number carries a sign (50 = neither positive nor negative) and the letter is the rank, so read the two together. "9th of 30 stocks scored" is the stock's place on that item. A dashed badge is provisional (fewer than 30 stocks scored).
